# Before starting

Welcome. Before starting or resuming work, check what `hostname` outputs.

- If it ends in "clank", run whatever commands you need.
- Otherwise, stop and ask the user to edit this file.

If this machine is too overloaded for benchmarks, ssh into `aclank`.

# Environment

All thinking is hidden from the user, so if you find anything they may wish to know about, please write to the output.

Your `Bash` tool uses zsh, not bash.

You're on NixOS and many things are installed, including:

ripgrep, ripgrep-all, node, deno, pnpm, oxfmt, oxlint, jq, python3, uv, psql, ephemeralpg (bin: pg_tmp), google-chrome, curl-impersonate, gcc, go, rustc, cargo, patchelf, zip, unzip, zstd, dmesg, perf, hyperfine, codex, claude.

Third-party binaries may fail with ENOENT and thus need patching for NixOS:

	patchelf --set-interpreter "$(patchelf --print-interpreter /bin/sh)" BIN

plus `--set-rpath` to a nix gcc-lib for libstdc++ if needed.

When waiting on something, avoid `sleep N` where N > 10; use built-in task watching or e.g. `wait-for-process-exit PID`, or loop something e.g. `rg -q PATTERN FILE` with a 2 second wait.

To run commands in the background and then wait for them, end each command with `&` directly (not `( command & )`, because `wait` doesn't wait for a command inside a subshell), then run `wait` in the same shell. Never wait in a loop on `pgrep -f PATTERN`: the looping shell's own command line contains PATTERN, so `pgrep` keeps finding that shell and the loop never ends.

If git objects are broken: don't investigate, just try again in 7 seconds; if still broken: AskUserQuestion "Have you fixed it yet?" Y/N.

# Avoid consuming tokens in excess

Use `rg` in various ways until you know you need the rest of the file.

If you're Claude and are spending a lot of time in hairy / complex code, ask Astra for help, with `run_in_background` (Astra can take several minutes):

	codex exec -c model="gpt-6.2-astra" -c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh" -s read-only - 2> LOG_FILE <<'EOF'
	PROMPT
	EOF

Keep the prompt in the quoted heredoc. The shell then expands nothing in the prompt, and `codex exec` gets a stdin that ends (given a stdin that never ends, `codex exec` waits forever). Stdout gets only Astra's answer; LOG_FILE gets everything else that Astra did.

# Thoughts for when there is programming involved

We want a coherent, maintainable artifact that humans are happy with.

A program can be:
- shorter.
- easier to read by a human.
- more correct around edge cases.
- faster than another which does the same thing.
- much easier to change when the requirements change.

These are sometimes in conflict.

Try writing a function in different ways and see which version is better.

Sometimes a program can log or assert to generate interesting observations which feed into further development of the program. We do our own science on the outputs later to improve the program.

When there are multiple good ways to implement something, especially involving state or the definition of a type: please ask the user. User loves AskUserQuestion, but please explain the problem correctly in the regular session before asking the question.

# This fork

This repository is a fork of upstream libtorrent (github.com/arvidn/libtorrent; the remote `upstream`). The fork's work is on `prime`: a commit of upstream's `RC_2_0` branch (0a49da5d07a9, the tag `v2.0.16`, as of 2026-11) plus the fork's own commits. `git log --oneline upstream/RC_2_0..prime` lists those commits, and each subject says what its commit changes. The fork's remote is `origin` (github.com/ludios/libtorrent); push to it only when the user asks.

The user's machines get libtorrent from the user's nixpkgs fork in `~/code/system/nixpkgs`. Its `pkgs/by-name/li/libtorrent-rasterbar-2_0_x/package.nix` fetches one commit of `prime` from github.com/ludios/libtorrent (by `rev` and `hash`), and the user's qBittorrent fork (`~/code/system/qbittorrent`) is built against that package. A new commit on `prime` therefore changes nothing on the user's machines until it is pushed to `origin` and that `package.nix` names it. Keep `prime` on upstream's 2.0 series (`RC_2_0`): libtorrent 2.1 (upstream's `RC_2_1` and `master`) removed `storage_params::mapped_files`, which this qBittorrent uses. Nix rebuilds each package that depends on this one whenever this one changes, so the fork's commits may change the ABI, which upstream's `.github/CONTRIBUTING.rst` forbids on upstream's `RC_*` branches.

To move `prime` to a newer upstream commit, `git fetch upstream`, then rebase `prime` onto that commit of `upstream/RC_2_0` (the rules in "Using git safely" apply).

Keep each of the fork's changes small and in a commit of its own, so that `prime` rebases with few conflicts. Follow the pull request checklist in upstream's `.github/CONTRIBUTING.rst` (for example: a test in `test/`, or a simulation in `simulation/`, for each change of behavior; and each new file in `Jamfile`, `Makefile` and `CMakeLists.txt`), except for its `ChangeLog` entries: the top of `ChangeLog` changes with each upstream release, so an entry there would conflict in each rebase. Follow the style of the code around each change (tabs for indentation, `TORRENT_ASSERT`), and change as few of upstream's lines as you can: each changed line can conflict in a later rebase.

# Before committing

Before committing a change to the code, build libtorrent and its tests with the debug checks of upstream's CI (assertions, full invariant checks, and libstdc++'s checked iterators), in the build environment of the system's nixpkgs package, and run the tests:

	git submodule update --init --recursive
	nix-shell '<nixpkgs>' -A libtorrent-rasterbar-2_0_x --run '
		cmake -B cmake-build-debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -Dbuild_tests=ON \
			-Ddeveloper-options=ON -Dasserts=on -Dinvariant-checks=full -Ddebug-iterators=ON &&
		cmake --build cmake-build-debug --parallel "$(nproc)" &&
		cd cmake-build-debug && ctest -j8 --timeout 600'

The `git submodule` command changes nothing where the submodules are checked out already, but a new clone (a `git clone --shared` copy, too) needs it: both builds use `deps/try_signal`, and the simulations use `simulation/libsimulator`.

`<nixpkgs>` is the nixpkgs that the system was built from (`/var/nixpkgs`, through `NIX_PATH`), so nix normally finds every dependency in the store already. Don't use `nix-shell ~/code/system/nixpkgs` instead: that checkout is often ahead of the system. The CMake build type `Debug` passes no `-O` option, so nixpkgs' compiler wrapper adds `-O2` (for its `fortify` hardening). To debug a test in gdb, build in another `cmake-build-*` directory with `export NIX_HARDENING_ENABLE=` before the `cmake` commands, which turns off the hardening, and with it the `-O2`.

Then build the tests with deprecated functions off, as upstream's CI also does:

	nix-shell '<nixpkgs>' -A libtorrent-rasterbar-2_0_x --run '
		cmake -B cmake-build-no-deprecated -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -Dbuild_tests=ON -Ddeprecated-functions=OFF &&
		cmake --build cmake-build-no-deprecated --parallel "$(nproc)"'

Then run upstream's simulations (`simulation/`: tests that run in a simulated network, in simulated time, which only b2 builds), as upstream's CI does:

	nix-shell -p boost boost-build --run '
		cd simulation &&
		NIX_HARDENING_ENABLE= b2 -j"$(nproc)" debug-iterators=on invariant-checks=full asserts=on picker-debugging=on'

Without `NIX_HARDENING_ENABLE=`, nixpkgs' compiler wrapper causes two warnings in each file that b2 compiles at `-O0` (`_FORTIFY_SOURCE requires compiling with optimization` and `"_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE" redefined`). b2 runs only the tests whose files changed since its last run, prints `**passed**` for each test that it runs and that passes, and exits with status 0 only if no test failed.

On xclank in 2026-11, while other work was loading it, the debug build took 3 minutes from an empty `cmake-build-debug/`, its `ctest` took 1.5 minutes, the build with deprecated functions off took 4 minutes from an empty `cmake-build-no-deprecated/`, and the simulations took 3 minutes when b2 had built nothing yet. All of these builds put their output in directories that `.gitignore` lists (`cmake-build-*/`, and b2's `bin/` directories).

`ctest` counts each test binary (`cmake-build-debug/test/test_NAME`, built from `test/test_NAME.cpp`) as one test. Because of a bug in upstream's test runner, the output of a binary (which `ctest` saves) shows only the first of its failing test cases, unless the binary is run with `-n`. In `cmake-build-debug/test/` (the test binaries look for their data files relative to it), `./test_NAME -l` lists a binary's test cases, and `./test_NAME CASE...` runs only the cases named. Name each case exactly as `-l` prints it: the absolute path of the source file, then `.` and the case's name. For example:

	cd cmake-build-debug/test
	./test_resume -n "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/test/test_resume.cpp.all_pieces_alerts"

Don't add compiler warnings: upstream's CI builds with `warnings-as-errors=on`. As of 2026-11, the debug build from an empty `cmake-build-debug/` prints 3 warnings (`-Warray-bounds` twice and `-Wstringop-overflow` once), and the compiler prints none for the simulations (b2 itself warns about its configuration). An incremental build recompiles only the files that changed, and those that include them, so look for warnings in those files.

The builds and every test must pass, except for these test cases of 2 of `ctest`'s 107 tests, which fail as of 2026-11 without any change of yours (they fail the same way with deprecated functions off, and every simulation passes). Run these 2 binaries with `-n`, and check that no other case of theirs fails:

- `test_torrent_info`: 7 cases (`sanitize_path_trailing_dots`, `sanitize_path_trailing_spaces`, `sanitize_path`, `sanitize_path_force`, `sanitize_path_colon`, `parse_torrents` and `set_metadata_resolve_duplicate_filenames`; 20 failed checks in all) still expect a file name on Linux to keep its trailing dots and spaces, and characters such as `:` and `?`. The fork's commit "Forbid Windows-invalid characters in filenames even when running on Linux" makes Linux remove or replace them, as Windows does.
- `test_upnp`: 3 cases (`upnp_wipconn`, `upnp_wanipconnection` and `upnp_wanipconnection2`) get no answer to their UPnP search over multicast on the user's machines, with and without the fork's commits.

# Using git safely

**Other sessions may be staging and committing** here, including the files you are changing, and their edits can land between your last check and your commit. So, never use `git add FILE`, `git commit -a`, or `git commit -- FILES`. Instead, in the repository's top directory (elsewhere, a patch can silently miss files):

1. Write your changes to a patch, then remove any hunks that aren't yours:

		git diff --binary -- FILES > /tmp/NAME.patch

   `git diff` leaves out files that git doesn't track yet, so for each file you created, append:

		git diff --no-index --binary /dev/null NEW_FILE >> /tmp/NAME.patch

   This one exits with status 1 even on success, so don't chain it with `&&`.
2. If `git status` shows any change that you didn't make, run checks in a `git clone --shared` copy with only your patch applied.
3. Commit the patch through the index:

		git diff --cached --quiet && git apply --cached /tmp/NAME.patch && git commit -F /tmp/NAME.msg

   `git diff --cached --quiet` ensures no other session has staged anything, because `git commit` would commit that too. If `git apply` fails, HEAD has changed under your patch: remake it and test it again.

On HEAD, git rebase, amend, reset, stash, etc. **are never allowed**, unless other sessions are idle and not waiting on anything!

To change a commit message, use `git-reword COMMIT < NEW_FULL_MESSAGE`, not `git history reword` or an amend.

# Commit sizes and messages

Smaller changes are usually easier to think about. Commit one logical change at a time whenever possible! Commit early and often!

When small commits are too hard with e.g. the build still working, larger commits are fine.

**Use the imperative mood in the subject line**. Do not end the subject line with a period. Wrap the body at 72 characters, generally.

Commit IDs written to a file, commit message, or chat must have >= 12 chars to avoid ambiguity later.

Sample subject line:

	Don't insert a file and rollback a transaction just to get the id
	Factor out file-reading function that looks up the storage
	Make sure zstd-compressed data round-trips back to input data
	Refactor some tests a bit
	Refactor to reduce repetition
	Resolve oxlint warning
	schema: forbid '.' and '..' in DOMAIN linux_basename; add more tests
	storage_read::read: don't require storage for size=0 files
	storage_write::write: don't hold a postgres transaction open while we upload a file
	storage_write::write: don't take a transaction as an argument
	Tweak comment
	Update Cargo.lock

Automatically commit your changes with this commit template:

	Subject line

	A longer description or explanation of why/what is changing, when it is genuinely helpful.

	Model-output: model name e.g. Claude Mythos 5.2

	Session-file: ~/.claude/projects/[...]/[...].jsonl

# Code review after each commit

After each commit made, get it reviewed by Codex and by Claude, at xhigh reasoning effort (but Claude's fallback model at a lower effort), by running this in the repository, in one Bash call with `run_in_background` (the reviews can take many minutes):

	review-commits <sha>

If you made several commits, ensure reviews cover them all: either run `review-commits <sha>` once for each commit, or review the whole batch at once with `review-commits <sha before your first commit>..<sha of your last commit>`.

`review-commits` runs the reviewers in a `git clone --shared` of the repository, saves each review in ~/.ai-code-reviews, and prints every review, each under a line with the path of its file. Once every reviewer has exited, it deletes the clone, and exits with status 1 if any reviewer failed.

Notes:

- Review findings are from **fallible machines eager to find issues**: think and prefer fixes that don't add a bunch of code we don't really need.
- Once all the reviews are in, fix the oversights that are really worth fixing, in logical, independent commits where possible, without "act on the ... reviews of ..."! If nothing, say briefly why the findings didn't warrant changes.
- Do _not_ send follow-up fixes through another review. (Exception: the follow-up grew into something substantial beyond addressing the findings.)
